subject: pathology
title: Cellular Proliferation, Stem Cell Niches, and VEGF-Driven Angiogenesis

steps.tx: Following tissue injury and resolution of acute inflammation, the body restores architectural integrity through tissue repair. Repair proceeds through two coordinated processes: regeneration, which replaces damaged tissue with identical native parenchymal cells, and **scar formation**, which replaces unregenerated parenchymal defects with dense fibrous collagenous connective tissue.
steps.say: Tissue repair restores injured tissue through parenchymal regeneration or fibrous scar formation.

nodes.label: Acute Ischemic, Toxic, or Mechanical Damage Kills Local Parenchymal Cells
Integrity of Underlying Extracellular Matrix Scaffolding Assessed
Intact Matrix Allows Complete Parenchymal Regeneration by Stem Cells
Disrupted Basement Membrane Mandates Granulation Tissue and Scar Formation

steps.tx: The intrinsic regenerative capacity of any organ depends fundamentally on the proliferative classification of its constituent cells. Divided according to mitotic turnover, human tissues comprise continuously dividing labile tissues, quiescent **stable tissues**, and non-dividing permanent tissues that have permanently exited the cell cycle.
steps.say: Human tissues are classified by regenerative potential into labile, stable, and permanent tissues.

left.title: Labile (Continuously Dividing) Cells
points: Continuously proliferate throughout adult life to replace shed cells
Derived from self-renewing resident tissue stem cell pools
Examples: hematopoietic bone marrow stem cells, oral mucosal epithelium
Epidermis, gastrointestinal crypt epithelium, and urinary tract transitional cells

right.title: Stable (Quiescent) Cells
points: Normally quiescent in G0 phase with low baseline mitotic turnover
Capable of rapid reentry into G1 phase upon injury or growth factor drive
Examples: hepatic parenchyma, renal tubular cells, pancreatic acini
Vascular endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells

steps.tx: In contrast to labile and stable tissues, permanent cells cannot undergo mitotic division in postnatal life. Comprising nerve cells within the central nervous system, skeletal muscle fibers, and **ventricular cardiomyocytes**, irreversible necrosis in permanent tissues cannot be restored by parenchymal replication, repairing exclusively through permanent fibrous scar tissue.
steps.say: Permanent tissues like cardiac myocytes cannot divide, healing exclusively through fibrous scarring.

left.title: Permanent (Non-Dividing) Cells
points: Terminally differentiated and permanently exited cell cycle into G0
Cannot undergo mitotic division following ischemic or physical injury
Neurons in central nervous system and cardiac ventricular myocytes
Irreversible cell death heals strictly through fibrous scarring or gliosis

right.title: Hepatic Regenerative Capacity (Stable)
points: Hepatocytes reside in G0 phase but retain massive proliferative reserve
Following 60% partial hepatectomy, remaining liver regenerates fully within weeks
Driven by priming cytokines (IL-6, TNF) and growth factors (HGF, TGF-alpha)
Terminates precisely when original liver mass is restored via antiproliferative TGF-beta

steps.tx: Parenchymal regeneration and fibrous repair are driven by soluble polypeptide growth factors that bind specific cell-surface receptors. Most growth factors, such as epidermal growth factor and hepatocyte growth factor, bind **receptor tyrosine kinases**, autophosphorylating cytoplasmic tyrosine residues to fire Ras-MAP kinase cascades that promote cell cycle entry.
steps.say: Growth factors bind receptor tyrosine kinases, firing Ras-MAP kinase to drive cell division.

nodes.label: Polypeptide Growth Factor (EGF, HGF, PDGF) Binds Extracellular Receptor Domain
Induces Receptor Dimerization and Cytoplasmic Tyrosine Autophosphorylation
Recruits GRB2/SOS to Activate Membrane-Bound Ras GTPase and MAP Kinase
Transcription Factors (c-Myc, c-Jun) Induce Cyclin D, Driving G0-to-S Phase Entry

steps.tx: Repair of extensive tissue defects requires the growth of new blood vessels from existing vascular beds to supply oxygen and nutrients. Termed **angiogenesis or neovascularization**, this critical repair process is orchestrated by vascular endothelial growth factor-A, which binds VEGFR-two on endothelial tip cells to direct vessel sprouting.
steps.say: Angiogenesis sprouts new capillaries from existing vessels, orchestrated by VEGF-A binding VEGFR-2.

vis.caption: Subretinal choroidal neovascularization displaying uncontrolled VEGF-driven endothelial capillary sprouting.
vis.alt: Choroidal neovascular membrane formation driven by pathological VEGF secretion

steps.tx: During capillary sprouting, specialized endothelial tip cells sense VEGF gradients, extending filopodia to guide directional vessel migration. As the tip cell migrates, trailing stalk cells proliferate to form a functional vascular lumen, regulated by the **Notch signaling pathway** which ensures that only selected endothelial cells become active leading tip sprouts.
steps.say: VEGF stimulates endothelial tip cells, while Notch signaling suppresses adjacent cells to pattern sprouts.

nodes.label: HIF-1 Drives Massive Secretion of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF-A)
Endothelial Tip Cell Extends Motile Filopodia Toward the VEGF Gradient
Tip Cell Expresses Delta-Like Ligand 4, Activating Notch in Stalk Cells to Inhibit Sprouting

steps.tx: Newly formed angiogenic capillary vessels are initially leaky because endothelial intercellular junctions are immature and VEGF directly increases microvascular permeability. This persistent leakage explains why **healing granulation tissue** is characteristically edematous and why therapeutic anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies rapidly resolve pathological tissue edema in wet macular degeneration.
steps.say: Immature angiogenic vessels leak fluid into healing tissue, explaining why granulation beds are edematous.

left.title: Immature Angiogenic Capillaries
points: Endothelial cells express incomplete, loosely organized tight junctions
VEGF directly promotes hyperpermeability through vesicular vacuolar organelles
Paucicellular basement membrane lacking invested mural pericytes
Leads to continuous fluid exudation and clinical tissue edema

right.title: Vascular Maturation and Stabilization
points: Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF-BB) recruits stabilizing pericytes
Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) binds Tie-2 receptors, stabilizing endothelial junctions
Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) stimulates basement membrane assembly
Vessels mature into tight, non-leaking, structurally stable microvessels

steps.tx: Pathological neovascularization occurs when excessive, unregulated VEGF production drives abnormal, fragile vessel proliferation. In proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinal capillary ischemia drives hypoxia-inducible factor-one alpha stabilization, stimulating exuberant **retinal neovascularization** that bleeds into the vitreous cavity and causes tractional retinal detachment.
steps.say: Retinal ischemia stabilizes HIF-1, driving abnormal VEGF neovascularization in diabetic retinopathy.

vis.alt: Funduscopic view of proliferative diabetic retinopathy with neovascularization
